Physiology-05.question: ১) Which of the following area is concerned with the movement of eyes?
Physiology-05.exp:
The occipital eye field (visual eye field) is concerned with voluntary movement of the eyes, especially coordinating visual tracking movements. It is located in the occipital lobe and helps control eye movements in response to visual stimuli.

Why others are incorrect:

  • Primary visual area  → Located in the occipital lobe (area 17); responsible for receiving and processing visual information, not eye movement.

  • Visual association area  → Interprets and recognizes visual information (shape, color, objects).

  • Pretectal nucleus  → Involved mainly in the pupillary light reflex.

Exam pearl:

  • Eye movement → Occipital eye field (visual eye field)

  • Vision perception → Primary visual cortex (Area 17)

  • Visual interpretation → Visual association cortex (Areas 18 & 19)

  • Pupillary reflex → Pretectal nucleus

Physiology-05.question: ২) Which of the following is not a pupillary reflex?
Physiology-05.exp:
Geniculoptic reflex is not a pupillary reflex. It is not a recognized reflex pathway involving changes in pupil size.

Pupillary reflexes include:

  • Light reflex → Constriction of pupil in response to light (direct & consensual)

  • Accommodation reflex → Pupil constriction during near vision along with lens accommodation

  • Ciliospinal reflex → Pupillary dilation in response to painful skin stimulation (sympathetic reflex)

Why others are incorrect:

  • Light reflex  → A true pupillary reflex.

  • Ciliospinal reflex  → A sympathetic pupillary reflex.

  • Accommodation reflex  → A pupillary near response.

Exam pearl:

  • Pupillary reflexes → Light, accommodation, ciliospinal

  • Geniculoptic reflex → Not a pupillary reflex

Physiology-05.question: ৩) Which of the following does not support accommodation reflex?
Physiology-05.option3: Contraction of constrictor pupillae of iris
Physiology-05.option4: Increase in the anterior curvature of the lens
Physiology-05.exp:
Accommodation reflex for near vision involves three coordinated responses (near triad):

  1. Contraction of ciliary muscle → relaxes zonular fibers → lens becomes more convex.

  2. Contraction of constrictor pupillae (sphincter pupillae) → pupil constriction.

  3. Contraction of medial recti muscles → convergence of eyes.

Therefore, relaxation of the ciliary muscle does not support accommodation; it occurs during viewing distant objects.

Why others are incorrect:

  • Contraction of medial recti  → Supports convergence during near vision.

  • Contraction of constrictor pupillae of iris  → Causes miosis, improving near focus.

  • Increase in anterior curvature of lens  → Makes lens more convex for near vision.

Exam pearl:
Accommodation reflex (near triad):

  • Ciliary muscle contraction

  • Pupil constriction

  • Medial rectus contraction
    → Lens becomes more convex for near vision.

Physiology-05.question: ৪) Which of the followings act as centre for accommodation?
Physiology-05.exp:
The centre for accommodation reflex is the Edinger–Westphal nucleus, which is the parasympathetic nucleus of the oculomotor nerve (CN III).

During accommodation:

  • Edinger–Westphal nucleus activates ciliary muscle contraction → lens becomes more convex.

  • Causes constriction of pupil via sphincter pupillae.

  • Helps in near vision.

Exam pearl:

  • Accommodation reflex centre → Edinger–Westphal nucleus

  • Light reflex → Pretectal nucleus → Edinger–Westphal nucleus

  • Primary visual cortex → Brodmann area 17

  • Visual association cortex → Brodmann areas 18 & 19

Physiology-05.question: ৫) Which of the following is the amplitude of accommodation at 50 years age?
Physiology-05.exp:
Amplitude of accommodation is the maximum increase in the refractive power of the eye produced by the lens during near vision. It decreases progressively with age due to reduced elasticity of the lens (presbyopia).

Approximate amplitude of accommodation:

  • 10 years → 14 D

  • 20 years → 10 D

  • 30 years → 7 D

  • 40 years → 4 D

  • 50 years → 1–2 D

  • 60 years → 0 D

Therefore, at 50 years of age, the amplitude of accommodation is approximately 1.0 D.

Exam pearl:

  • Accommodation decreases with age

  • Presbyopia occurs due to loss of lens elasticity

  • At 50 years → Accommodation ≈ 1 D

Physiology-05.question: ৬) Which of the followings is not the feature of oculosympathetic palsy?
Physiology-05.exp:
Oculosympathetic palsy (Horner syndrome) occurs due to interruption of the sympathetic supply to the eye. Its classical features are:

  • Ptosis → due to paralysis of superior tarsal (Müller) muscle

  • Miosis → due to loss of sympathetic dilator pupillae activity

  • Swelling of lower eyelid / apparent enophthalmos → due to loss of sympathetic tone

Exophthalmos is not a feature of oculosympathetic palsy; it is more commonly associated with hyperthyroidism (Graves’ disease).

Exam pearl:
Horner syndrome = Ptosis + Miosis + Anhidrosis + Apparent enophthalmos
Sympathetic loss → Small pupil (miosis)
Sympathetic overactivity → Dilated pupil (mydriasis)

Physiology-05.question: ৭) Which of the followings act as third order neuron in Visual pathway?
Physiology-05.exp:
The third-order neuron of the visual pathway is located in the lateral geniculate body (LGB) of the thalamus.

Visual pathway sequence:

  1. First-order neuron → Bipolar cells of retina

  2. Second-order neuron → Ganglion cells of retina

  3. Third-order neuron → Lateral geniculate body

  4. Optic radiation → Primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17)

Exam pearl:

  • Retina → Optic nerve → Optic chiasma → Optic tract → Lateral geniculate body → Optic radiation → Visual cortex

  • Third-order neuron of vision → LGB

Physiology-05.question: ৮) Which of the following is true regarding Visual pathway?
Physiology-05.option1: Optic tract is formed by uncrossed fibers of optic nerve on the same side and crossed fibers of optic nerve from the opposite side
Physiology-05.option2: Fibers from fovea enter superior colliculus
Physiology-05.option3: Supraoptic nucleus of hypothalamus is concerned with the retinal control of pituitary in human
Physiology-05.option4: Fibers from geniculate body pass through external capsule
Physiology-05.exp:
The optic tract contains:

  • Uncrossed fibers from the temporal half of the retina of the same eye

  • Crossed fibers from the nasal half of the retina of the opposite eye

These fibers carry visual information from the corresponding visual fields to the lateral geniculate body (LGB).

Exam pearl:

  • Nasal retinal fibers → Cross at optic chiasma

  • Temporal retinal fibers → Remain uncrossed

  • Optic tract → Contralateral visual field information

  • Optic radiation → Passes through internal capsule (not external capsule)

Physiology-05.question: ৯) Which of the followings occur as a result of lesion of lateral fibers in left side of optic chiasma?
Physiology-05.exp:
The lateral fibers of the optic chiasma contain uncrossed temporal retinal fibers. A lesion of the left lateral side of optic chiasma affects the left temporal retinal fibers, which carry information from the left nasal visual field.

Therefore, the result is left nasal hemianopia.

However, among the given options, the classic lesion of the lateral fibers of both sides of optic chiasma produces binasal hemianopia.

Exam pearl:

  • Central optic chiasma lesion (crossed nasal fibers) → Bitemporal hemianopia (e.g., pituitary tumor)

  • Lateral optic chiasma lesion (uncrossed temporal fibers) → Binasal hemianopia

  • Optic tract lesion → Contralateral homonymous hemianopia

Physiology-05.question: ১০) Which of the followings does not form the pathway of light reflex?
Physiology-05.exp:
Explanation :

Ref : Sembulingam 6th edition (Figure- 169.1)

Physiology-05.question: ১১) Which of the followings is false regarding accommodation reflex?
Physiology-05.exp:
The accommodation reflex helps the eye focus on near objects by increasing the curvature of the lens. It produces several optical effects:

  • Increases visual acuity  → More accurate focusing of near objects.

  • Reduces lateral chromatic aberrations  → Improves image quality.

  • Increases depth of focus  → Due to pupil constriction (miosis), which improves near vision.

However, accommodation reduces spherical aberrations, not increases them. A more rounded lens during accommodation improves focusing ability.

Exam pearl:
Accommodation reflex (near triad):

  • Ciliary muscle contraction

  • Lens becomes more convex

  • Pupil constriction

  • Medial rectus contraction

Effects:
 ↑ Visual acuity
 ↑ Depth of focus
 ↓ Spherical aberration
 ↑ Spherical aberration is false

Physiology-05.question: ১২) Which of the followings is 2nd order neuron in auditory pathway?
Physiology-05.exp:
In the auditory pathway, the second-order neuron is located in the ventral and dorsal cochlear nuclei in the brainstem.

Auditory pathway sequence:

  1. First-order neuron → Bipolar cells of spiral ganglion (cochlear nerve, CN VIII)

  2. Second-order neuron → Cochlear nuclei (ventral & dorsal)

  3. Fibers project to superior olivary nucleus (third-order relay)

  4. Lateral lemniscus → Inferior colliculus → Medial geniculate body → Auditory cortex

Exam pearl:

  • 1st order neuron → Spiral ganglion

  • 2nd order neuron → Cochlear nucleus

  • 3rd order neuron → Medial geniculate body

  • Primary auditory cortex → Superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann area 41, 42)

Physiology-05.question: ১৩) Which of the followings is known as auditopsychic area?
Physiology-05.exp:
The auditopsychic area is the Wernicke’s area, which is responsible for interpretation and understanding of spoken language (auditory association).

  • Located in the dominant hemisphere (usually left side).

  • Corresponds mainly to Brodmann area 22 (posterior part of superior temporal gyrus).

Exam pearl:

  • Primary auditory cortex → Brodmann areas 41 & 42

  • Auditopsychic area / auditory association cortex → Wernicke’s area (Area 22)

  • Broca’s area → Motor speech production (Area 44, 45)

Physiology-05.question: ১৪) Which of the followings act as taste recptor cell in taste bud?
Physiology-05.exp:
The taste receptor cells in taste buds are mainly Type II cells and Type III cells.

  • Type II cells → Act as primary taste receptor cells for sweet, bitter, and umami tastes through G-protein coupled receptors.

  • Type III cells → Detect sour taste and form synapses with sensory nerve fibers.

  • Type I cells → Supportive/glial-like cells.

Exam pearl:

  • Taste receptor cell → Type II cell (major)

  • Sour taste → Type III cell

  • Supporting cell → Type I cell

  • Taste bud nerve supply → Facial nerve (anterior 2/3 tongue), Glossopharyngeal nerve (posterior 1/3)

Physiology-05.question: ১৫) Where is taste center situated?
Physiology-05.exp:
The taste centre (gustatory cortex) is located in the opercular insular cortex of the cerebral cortex. It is responsible for conscious perception and interpretation of taste sensations.

Taste pathway:
Taste buds → CN VII, IX, X → Nucleus of tractus solitarius (NTS) → Thalamus (VPM nucleus) → Opercular insular cortex (taste centre)

Exam pearl:

  • Primary taste centre → Opercular insular cortex

  • First central relay of taste → Nucleus of tractus solitarius

  • Thalamic relay → Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus

Physiology-05.question: ১৬) Receptor organ in otoliths is known as -
Physiology-05.exp:
The receptor organ in the otolith organs (utricle and saccule) is called the macula.

  • Macula of utricle → detects horizontal linear acceleration and head tilt.

  • Macula of saccule → detects vertical linear acceleration.

The macula contains hair cells covered by an otolithic membrane containing calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths/otoconia).

Exam pearl:

  • Otolith organs → Utricle + Saccule

  • Receptor → Macula

  • Semicircular canals → Crista ampullaris (angular acceleration)

  • Otoliths → Linear acceleration + gravity sensing

Physiology-05.question: ১৭) Which of the followings is true regarding vestibular apparatus?
Physiology-05.option1: Superior semicircular canal gives response to rotation in vertical axis
Physiology-05.option2: Horizontal semicircular canal gives response to rotation in transverse axis
Physiology-05.option3: Semicircular canals are concerned with linear acceleration
Physiology-05.option4: Otolith organ is concerned with acceleration in both horizontal and vertical planes
Physiology-05.exp:
The otolith organs (utricle and saccule) detect linear acceleration in different planes:

  • Utricle → Horizontal plane (forward/backward, side-to-side acceleration)

  • Saccule → Vertical plane (upward/downward acceleration)

The semicircular canals detect angular (rotational) acceleration, not linear acceleration.

Exam pearl:

  • Semicircular canals → Angular acceleration (rotation)

    • Horizontal canal → Rotation around vertical axis

    • Superior & posterior canals → Rotation in vertical planes

  • Otolith organs (utricle + saccule) → Linear acceleration + head position relative to gravity

Physiology-05.question: ১৮) Which of the following is a component of diencephalon?
Physiology-05.exp:
The diencephalon is a part of the forebrain and includes:

  • Thalamus

  • Hypothalamus

  • Epithalamus

  • Subthalamus

The hypothalamus is involved in:

  • Autonomic regulation

  • Endocrine control through the pituitary gland

  • Temperature regulation

  • Hunger, thirst, and circadian rhythm

Exam pearl:

  • Diencephalon → Thalamus + Hypothalamus + Epithalamus + Subthalamus

  • Basal ganglia, hippocampus, and amygdaloid nucleus → Telencephalon (cerebrum)

Physiology-05.question: ১৯) Which of the followings does not form brain stem?
Physiology-05.exp:
The brainstem is formed by three parts:

  • Mesencephalon (midbrain)

  • Pons

  • Myelencephalon (medulla oblongata)

The cerebellum does not form the brainstem. It is a separate part of the hindbrain involved in coordination of movement, balance, and posture.

Exam pearl:

  • Brainstem = Midbrain (Mesencephalon) + Pons + Medulla (Myelencephalon)

  • Cerebellum → Hindbrain, but not a component of brainstem

Physiology-05.question: ২০) Tigroid substances is absent from -
Physiology-05.exp:
Tigroid substances (Nissl bodies) are aggregates of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes present in the soma (cell body) and dendrites of neurons. They are responsible for protein synthesis.

Nissl bodies are absent in the axon hillock and axon, allowing the axon hillock to initiate action potentials.

Exam pearl:

  • Nissl bodies present → Soma + Dendrites

  • Nissl bodies absent → Axon hillock + Axon

  • Axon hillock → Site of action potential initiation

Physiology-05.question: ২১) Which of the followings is used to treat Parkinson's disease?
Physiology-05.exp:
Glial Cell Line-derived Neurotrophic Factor (GDNF) is studied and used therapeutically in Parkinson’s disease because it supports the survival and function of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, which are progressively lost in Parkinson’s disease.

Parkinson’s disease occurs due to degeneration of:

  • Dopamine-producing neurons of substantia nigra pars compacta

  • Reduced dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway

Exam pearl:

  • Parkinson’s disease → Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra

  • Neurotrophic factor associated with Parkinson’s treatment → GDNF

  • Main drug therapy → Levodopa + Carbidopa

Physiology-05.question: ২২) Which of the followings is the fastest conducting nerve fibres?
Physiology-05.exp:
Type A alpha (Aα) nerve fibres are the fastest conducting nerve fibres because they have:

  • Largest diameter

  • Thickest myelin sheath

They conduct impulses at approximately 80–120 m/s and are responsible for:

  • Proprioception (position sense)

  • Motor innervation of skeletal muscles

  • Touch and pressure sensations

Exam pearl:
Nerve fibre conduction velocity order:

Type Aα > Type Aβ > Type Aδ > Type B > Type C

  • Fastest → Aα fibres

  • Slowest → C fibres (unmyelinated pain fibres)

  • C fibres → slow, dull pain and temperature sensation

Physiology-05.question: ২৩) Which of the followings is not the property of nerve fibre?
Physiology-05.exp:
A nerve fibre does not show fatigability. Nerve fibres can conduct impulses repeatedly without getting fatigued because they have a high capacity for energy supply and ion pump activity.

Properties of nerve fibres include:

  • Summation → ability of repeated stimuli to produce a stronger response (mainly seen in neuronal circuits)

  • Adaptation → reduced response to a continuous stimulus

  • Relative refractory period → period after an action potential when stronger-than-normal stimulus is required

Exam pearl:

  • Nerve fibre properties: Excitability, conductivity, refractoriness, adaptation

  • Fatigability → characteristic of muscle, especially skeletal muscle during prolonged activity

  • Nerve fibres are not fatigable

Physiology-05.question: ২৪) What is the resting membrane potential of a nerve fibre?
Physiology-05.exp:
The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a nerve fibre is approximately −70 mV.

It is maintained by:

  • Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump → moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in

  • Higher permeability of membrane to K⁺ through potassium leak channels

  • Unequal distribution of ions across the membrane

At rest, the inside of the neuron is negatively charged compared to the outside.

Exam pearl:

  • Resting membrane potential of nerve fibre → −70 mV

  • Threshold potential → −55 mV

  • Peak action potential → +35 mV

  • Skeletal muscle resting potential → about −90 mV

Physiology-05.question: ২৫) Which of the followings is included in axonotmesis?
Physiology-05.exp:
Axonotmesis is a type of nerve injury in which there is disruption of the axon and myelin sheath, but the connective tissue coverings (endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium) remain intact. This corresponds to Seddon’s second-degree nerve injury.

Classification of nerve injury (Seddon):

  • Neurapraxia (1st degree) → Temporary conduction block, axon intact

  • Axonotmesis (2nd degree) → Axonal disruption with preserved connective tissue

  • Neurotmesis (3rd degree) → Complete nerve transection

Exam pearl:

  • 1st degree → Neurapraxia

  • 2nd degree → Axonotmesis

  • 3rd degree → Neurotmesis

  • Axonotmesis → Wallerian degeneration occurs distal to injury

Physiology-05.question: ২৬) Which of the followings play important role in blood-brain barrier formation?
Physiology-05.exp:
Explanation:
The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is mainly formed by:

  • Tight junctions between capillary endothelial cells

  • Basement membrane

  • Astrocyte end-feet (perivascular feet)

Among neuroglial cells, protoplasmic astrocytes (found mainly in gray matter) play an important role in maintaining the BBB by surrounding cerebral capillaries with their end-feet and regulating the exchange of substances between blood and brain tissue.

Exam pearl:

  • BBB formation → Endothelial tight junctions + Astrocyte end-feet

  • Astrocytes → Maintain BBB and support neurons

  • Oligodendrocytes → Myelin formation in CNS

  • Microglia → Phagocytic immune cells of CNS

Physiology-05.question: ২৭) Which is the function of satellite cells in PNS?
Physiology-05.option1: Regulation of chemical environment of ECF around the PNS neurons
Physiology-05.option2: Provide myelination around the nerve fibers in PNS
Physiology-05.option3: Play important role in nerve regeneration
Physiology-05.option4: Remove cellular debris during regeneration by phagocytic activity
Physiology-05.exp:
Satellite cells are specialized glial cells of the PNS that surround the cell bodies of neurons in sensory ganglia (e.g., dorsal root ganglia) and autonomic ganglia.

Their main functions:

  • Maintain and regulate the chemical environment of extracellular fluid (ECF) around neuronal cell bodies.

  • Provide metabolic and structural support to neurons.

Exam pearl:

  • Satellite cells (PNS) → Support neuron cell bodies + regulate ECF

  • Schwann cells → Myelination of PNS nerve fibres

  • Schwann cells also help nerve regeneration and remove debris after injury

  • Microglia → Phagocytosis in CNS

Physiology-05.question: ২৮) Which exteroceptor is involved in pressure sensation?
Physiology-05.exp:
Explanation :

Ref : Sembulingam 6th edition (Figure-139.2)

Physiology-05.question: ২৯) Which is true for excitatory post synaptic potential?
Physiology-05.option3: It is transmitted into the axon of postsynaptic neuron
Physiology-05.exp:
Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is a graded potential produced in the postsynaptic neuron after neurotransmitter binding to receptors. It causes depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane and increases the chance of generating an action potential.

Features of EPSP:

  • It is graded (amplitude depends on stimulus strength) 

  • It is not propagated like an action potential 

  • It does not obey the all-or-none law 

  • It occurs mainly in the dendrites and soma; if threshold is reached, an action potential is generated at the axon hillock 

Exam pearl:

  • EPSP → Graded depolarization

  • Action potential → Propagated + all-or-none law

  • IPSP → Graded hyperpolarization

Physiology-05.question: ৩০) Where does feedforward synaptic inhibition occur?
Physiology-05.exp:
Feedforward synaptic inhibition occurs when an incoming excitatory signal activates an inhibitory interneuron, which then inhibits another neuron before it becomes active. This mechanism helps regulate motor activity and prevent excessive excitation.

A classic example is in the spinal cord, where:

  • An excitatory motor pathway activates an inhibitory interneuron.

  • The inhibitory interneuron suppresses activity of other neurons, helping coordinate movements.

Exam pearl:

  • Feedforward inhibition → Spinal cord interneuronal circuits

  • Reciprocal inhibition → Antagonistic muscles (e.g., contraction of flexor with relaxation of extensor)

  • Feedback inhibition → Renshaw cell inhibition of motor neurons

Physiology-05.question: ৩১) Normal duration of synaptic delay is-
Physiology-05.exp:
Synaptic delay is the time required for transmission of an impulse across a chemical synapse. The normal duration of synaptic delay is approximately 0.3–0.5 milliseconds.

It occurs due to:

  • Release of neurotransmitter from presynaptic terminal

  • Diffusion across synaptic cleft

  • Binding to postsynaptic receptors

  • Opening of ion channels and generation of postsynaptic potential

Exam pearl:

  • Normal synaptic delay → 0.3–0.5 ms

  • Chemical synapse → slower than electrical synapse

  • Electrical synapse → almost no synaptic delay

Physiology-05.question: ৩২) Which of the followings act as both excitatory & inhibitory neurotransmitter?
Physiology-05.exp:
Explanation :

Ref : Sembulingam 6th edition (Table- 141.1)

Physiology-05.question: ৩৩) Which of the following neurotransmitter is not found in retinna?
Physiology-05.exp:
The retina contains several neurotransmitters involved in visual signal processing:

  • Glutamate → Major neurotransmitter of photoreceptors and bipolar cells

  • Glycine → Inhibitory neurotransmitter of amacrine cells

  • Dopamine → Present in dopaminergic amacrine cells and involved in retinal adaptation

  • Serotonin → Not a typical neurotransmitter found in the retina

Exam pearl:

  • Retinal neurotransmitters: Glutamate, GABA, Glycine, Dopamine

  • Photoreceptors release → Glutamate

  • Amacrine cells → GABA/Glycine/Dopamine

  • Serotonin → Not considered a retinal neurotransmitter

Physiology-05.question: ৩৪) Which of the followings is false regarding source of acetylcholine?
Physiology-05.option4: Postganglionic sympathetic cholinergic nerves supplying apocrine sweat glands
Physiology-05.exp:
Acetylcholine (ACh) is released from:

  • All preganglionic autonomic neurons 

    • Preganglionic parasympathetic nerves

    • Preganglionic sympathetic nerves

  • Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons 

    • Release ACh onto target organs (muscarinic receptors)

  • Postganglionic sympathetic cholinergic fibres supplying sweat glands 

    • Release ACh (especially to eccrine sweat glands; some texts mention apocrine sweat glands)

Therefore, postganglionic parasympathetic nerve is actually a source of acetylcholine, so the given options make the question ambiguous.

If forced to choose the false option, the best answer is usually:

None of the above (not provided).

Exam pearl:

  • All preganglionic autonomic fibres → ACh

  • Postganglionic parasympathetic fibres → ACh

  • Most postganglionic sympathetic fibres → Noradrenaline

  • Sympathetic sweat gland fibres → ACh

Physiology-05.question: ৩৫) Which of the followings is true for neuromodulators?
Physiology-05.option3: Chemically they are amino acids,amine or others
Physiology-05.exp:
Explanation :

Ref : Sembulingam 6th edition (Table- 141.3)

Physiology-05.question: ৩৬) What is the root value for radial periosteal reflex?
Physiology-05.exp:
The radial periosteal reflex (also called brachioradialis reflex) is a deep tendon reflex elicited by tapping the styloid process of radius. It tests the integrity of the C5 and C6 spinal nerve roots, mainly C6.

Reflex pathway:

  • Afferent limb: Radial nerve → C5–C6 spinal segments

  • Centre: C5–C6 spinal cord

  • Efferent limb: Radial nerve → Brachioradialis muscle contraction

Exam pearl:

  • Biceps reflex → C5, C6 (mainly C5)

  • Radial periosteal/brachioradialis reflex → C5, C6 (mainly C6)

  • Triceps reflex → C7, C8 (mainly C7)

  • Supinator jerk → C5, C6

Physiology-05.question: ৩৭) Which of the followings is not a superficial cutaneous reflex?
Physiology-05.exp:
Superficial cutaneous reflexes are elicited by stimulation of the skin and involve contraction of underlying muscles.

Examples:

  • Scapular reflex → superficial cutaneous reflex 

  • Finger flexion reflex → superficial cutaneous reflex 

  • Gluteal reflex → superficial cutaneous reflex 

The bulbocavernous reflex is a deep visceral reflex, not a superficial cutaneous reflex. It involves contraction of the bulbocavernosus muscle after stimulation of the genital region and is used to assess sacral spinal cord segments (S2–S4).

Exam pearl:

  • Superficial reflexes → Abdominal, cremasteric, plantar, anal, scapular, gluteal

  • Bulbocavernous reflex → Deep reflex (S2–S4)

Physiology-05.question: ৩৮) In which reflex Afferent nerve is not trigeminal nerve?
Physiology-05.exp:
The afferent limb of most facial sensory reflexes is carried by the trigeminal nerve (CN V).

  • Corneal reflex → Afferent: Ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (V1) ✅

  • Conjunctival reflex → Afferent: Trigeminal nerve (V1) ✅

  • Nasal reflex → Afferent: Trigeminal nerve (V1/V2) ✅

  • Uvular reflex (gag reflex) → Afferent: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) ❌

The uvular/gag reflex involves:

  • Afferent limb → CN IX (glossopharyngeal nerve)

  • Efferent limb → CN X (vagus nerve)

Exam pearl:

  • Trigeminal afferent reflexes → Corneal, conjunctival, nasal

  • Gag reflex → CN IX afferent + CN X efferent

  • Corneal reflex → V1 → VII (afferent → efferent)

Physiology-05.question: ৩৯) Which is not a protopathic sensation?
Physiology-05.exp:
Protopathic sensation refers to crude, poorly localized sensations carried mainly by the anterolateral (spinothalamic) pathway.

Protopathic sensations include:

  • Pain sensation 

  • Temperature sensation (wide range) 

  • Crude touch and pressure sensation 

Kinesthetic sensation (sense of movement and position of joints) is a deep sensation carried by the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway, so it is not protopathic.

Exam pearl:

  • Protopathic → Pain + Temperature + Crude touch/pressure

  • Epicritic → Fine touch, vibration, two-point discrimination

  • Kinesthesia/proprioception → Dorsal column pathway

Physiology-05.question: ৪০) What is the feature of lower motor neuron lesion?
Physiology-05.option3: Fascicular twitch in EMG is absent
Physiology-05.exp:
Explanation :

Ref : Sembulingam 6th edition (Table-144.3)

Physiology-05.question: ৪১) Sleep & wakefulness is regulated by -
Physiology-05.exp:
The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus is the main regulator of the sleep–wake cycle and circadian rhythm.

The SCN receives light information from the retina through the retinohypothalamic tract and controls:

  • Circadian rhythm

  • Melatonin secretion from the pineal gland

  • Daily sleep–wake pattern

Other hypothalamic areas:

  • Anterior hypothalamus → Promotes sleep (sleep center)

  • Posterior hypothalamus → Promotes wakefulness (contains orexin/hypocretin neurons)

  • Lateral hypothalamus → Hunger regulation and arousal via orexin

Exam pearl:

  • Sleep–wake cycle regulator → Suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN)

  • Sleep center → Anterior hypothalamus

  • Wakefulness center → Posterior hypothalamus

Physiology-05.question: ৪২) What acts as satiety centre?
Physiology-05.exp:
The ventromedial nucleus (VMN) of the hypothalamus acts as the satiety centre. Activation of this centre produces a feeling of fullness and inhibits food intake.

Functions of hypothalamic feeding centres:

  • Ventromedial nucleus → Satiety centre (decreases eating)

  • Lateral hypothalamic nucleus → Hunger centre (stimulates eating)

Other nuclei:

  • Dorsomedial nucleus → Involved in feeding behaviour and autonomic regulation

  • Supraoptic nucleus → Produces ADH and oxytocin

Exam pearl:

  • Satiety centre → Ventromedial hypothalamus

  • Hunger centre → Lateral hypothalamus

  • Damage to VMN → Hyperphagia and obesity

  • Damage to lateral hypothalamus → Loss of appetite (aphagia)

Physiology-05.question: ৪৩) Which nuclei of hypothalamus is a part of tuberal group?
Physiology-05.exp:
The tuberal group of hypothalamic nuclei is located in the middle region of the hypothalamus and includes nuclei around the tuber cinereum.

The tuberal group includes:

  • Ventromedial nucleus

  • Dorsomedial nucleus

  • Lateral hypothalamic nucleus

Other options:

  • Mammillary body → Belongs to the posterior (mammillary) group

  • Paraventricular nucleus → Belongs to the anterior/supraoptic group

  • Anterior nuclei → Part of the anterior group

Exam pearl:
Hypothalamic nuclear groups:

  • Anterior group → Supraoptic, paraventricular, anterior nuclei

  • Tuberal group → Ventromedial, dorsomedial, lateral nuclei

  • Posterior group → Mammillary bodies

Physiology-05.question: ৪৪) Which acts as final common path of cerebellar cortex?
Physiology-05.exp:
Purkinje cells act as the final common pathway (final output pathway) of the cerebellar cortex.

They are the only neurons of the cerebellar cortex that send output signals from the cerebellar cortex to the deep cerebellar nuclei. Purkinje cells are inhibitory neurons and release GABA.

Other cerebellar cortical cells:

  • Stellate cells → Inhibitory interneurons acting on Purkinje cells

  • Basket cells → Inhibitory interneurons acting on Purkinje cells

  • Golgi cells → Inhibitory interneurons that regulate granule cells

Exam pearl:

  • Final common pathway of cerebellar cortex → Purkinje cell

  • Only output neuron of cerebellar cortex → Purkinje cell

  • Purkinje neurotransmitter → GABA (inhibitory)

Physiology-05.question: ৪৫) What is the excitatory cell of cerebellum?
Physiology-05.exp:
The granule cells are the excitatory cells of the cerebellum. They are the only excitatory neurons present in the cerebellar cortex and release glutamate as their neurotransmitter.

Granule cells:

  • Receive input from mossy fibres

  • Send parallel fibres to stimulate Purkinje cells

  • Produce excitatory effects in cerebellar circuits

Other cerebellar cells:

  • Basket cells → Inhibitory (GABAergic) interneurons

  • Golgi cells → Inhibitory (GABAergic) interneurons

  • Purkinje cells → Inhibitory (GABAergic) output neurons of cerebellar cortex

Exam pearl:

  • Excitatory cell of cerebellar cortex → Granule cell

  • Final output cell of cerebellar cortex → Purkinje cell

  • Purkinje neurotransmitter → GABA (inhibitory)

Physiology-05.question: ৪৬) Which of the followings is a polysynaptic reflex?
Physiology-05.exp:
A polysynaptic reflex involves one or more interneurons between the sensory neuron and motor neuron.

The flexor withdrawal reflex is a classic polysynaptic reflex because:

  • Painful stimulus activates sensory neurons

  • Signals pass through multiple interneurons in the spinal cord

  • Flexor muscles contract to withdraw the limb

Other reflexes:

  • Golgi tendon reflex → Polysynaptic (also involves interneuron), but the best classic answer is flexor withdrawal reflex

  • Clasp-knife reflex → UMN phenomenon due to sudden reduction of resistance after initial stretch

  • Stretch reflex → Monosynaptic reflex (e.g., knee jerk)

Exam pearl:

  • Stretch reflex → Monosynaptic

  • Flexor withdrawal reflex → Polysynaptic

  • Golgi tendon reflex → Polysynaptic

  • Withdrawal reflex protects from painful stimuli

Physiology-05.question: ৪৭) What is the function of vestibulocerebellum?
Physiology-05.exp:
The vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular lobe of cerebellum) is mainly responsible for maintenance of balance and equilibrium and coordination of eye movements.

Functions of cerebellar divisions:

  • Vestibulocerebellum → Balance, posture, equilibrium, eye movements

  • Spinocerebellum → Coordination and synergy of ongoing movements

  • Cerebrocerebellum → Planning and initiation of skilled movements

Other options:

  • Planning of movement → Cerebrocerebellum

  • Initiation of movement → Cerebrocerebellum (via motor cortex connections)

  • Synergy of movement → Spinocerebellum

Exam pearl:

  • Flocculonodular lobe = Vestibulocerebellum = Balance & equilibrium

  • Vermis/intermediate zone = Spinocerebellum = Posture & coordination

  • Lateral hemisphere = Cerebrocerebellum = Planning skilled movement

Physiology-05.question: ৪৮) Which of the following responses is mediated by parasympathetic muscarinic receptors?
Physiology-05.exp:
Parasympathetic actions are mainly mediated by muscarinic receptors and produce “rest and digest” effects.

Miosis (pupillary constriction) occurs due to activation of M3 muscarinic receptors on the sphincter pupillae muscle of the iris.

Other options:

  • Dilation of bronchiolar smooth muscle → Sympathetic β₂ effect causes bronchodilation; parasympathetic causes bronchoconstriction

  • Ejaculation → Mainly sympathetic α₁ adrenergic action

  • Constriction of gastrointestinal sphincters → Sympathetic action; parasympathetic generally relaxes sphincters and increases gut motility

Exam pearl:

  • Parasympathetic muscarinic M3 → Miosis, bronchoconstriction, increased GI motility, bladder contraction

  • Sympathetic → Ejaculation, bronchodilation, mydriasis

Physiology-05.question: ৪৯) Which of the following is a property of C fibers?
Physiology-05.option1: Have the smallest diameter of any nerve fiber type
Physiology-05.option2: Are afferent nerves from muscle spindles
Physiology-05.option3: Are afferent nerves from Golgi tendon organs
Physiology-05.exp:
C fibers are the smallest diameter nerve fibers and are unmyelinated, therefore they conduct impulses very slowly.

Features of C fibers:

  • Smallest diameter nerve fibers 

  • Unmyelinated fibers

  • Slow conduction velocity (about 0.5–2 m/s)

  • Carry slow pain, temperature, and itch sensations

  • Also include postganglionic sympathetic autonomic fibers

Other options:

  • Afferent nerves from muscle spindles → Mainly Group Ia (Aα fibers)

  • Afferent nerves from Golgi tendon organs → Group Ib (Aα fibers)

  • Preganglionic autonomic fibers → B fibers (small myelinated fibers)

Exam pearl:

  • C fibers → Smallest, unmyelinated, slow pain

  • Aα fibers → Fastest conduction, proprioception (muscle spindle/Golgi tendon)

  • B fibers → Preganglionic autonomic fibers

Physiology-05.question: ৫০) The inability to perform rapidly alternating movement is associated with lesions of the-
Physiology-05.exp:
The inability to perform rapidly alternating movements is called dysdiadochokinesia. It is a classic sign of a cerebellar lesion.

The cerebellum is responsible for:

  • Coordination of voluntary movements

  • Timing and precision of muscle activity

  • Smooth execution of rapid alternating movements

Other options:

  • Premotor cortex → Planning and preparation of movements

  • Motor cortex → Initiation and execution of voluntary movements

  • Substantia nigra → Dopamine production; lesion causes Parkinson’s disease with rigidity, tremor, and bradykinesia

Exam pearl:

  • Dysdiadochokinesia → Cerebellar lesion

  • Intention tremor → Cerebellar lesion

  • Resting tremor → Substantia nigra lesion (Parkinson’s disease)
